query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the SLM/LPBF processing parameters—specifically by increasing the scan speed and reducing the hatch spacing to enable controlled multi-pass remelting—will improve the dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of high-entropy alloy components by promoting a more homogeneous microstructure with decreased defect density.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy components produced via standard SLM/LPBF processes that exhibit fabrication-induced defects such as porosity, microsegregation, and non-uniform dislocation distributions.
generation.intervention: Tailor the process parameters by increasing the laser scan speed and reducing the hatch spacing, coupled with a selective multi-pass remelting strategy.
generation.conditions: This intervention applies during the additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn or AlCoCrFeNi) using SLM/LPBF machines with similar powder feedstock and environmental conditions as in prior studies.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined and homogenized microstructure featuring a uniform dislocation density, reduced porosity, and minimized microsegregation.
generation.mechanism: Higher scan speeds reduce heat accumulation while a reduced hatch spacing with controlled remelting promotes a uniform thermal profile. This combination minimizes local overheating and thermal gradients, thereby limiting defect formation such as porosity and non-uniform grain structures, which leads to improved mechanical performance and dimensional stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized process should yield components with better dimensional accuracy (lower distortion) and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength and more consistent hardness) compared to components fabricated under conventional processing conditions.
generation.baseline: Components manufactured using traditional SLM/LPBF parameters with standard scan speeds, hatch spacing, and without a controlled remelting step, which typically exhibit higher defect densities and less precise dimensions.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected within similar processing setups (e.g., same alloy system and machine capabilities). Deviations in material composition or significant changes in laser power and other fundamental parameters might alter the outcome.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement is uncertain as it may depend on the specific alloy system and machine setup. Systematic parameter optimization is necessary to identify the optimal combination for each high-entropy alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens using an SLM/LPBF system: one set under standard processing parameters and another set under the optimized parameters (increased scan speed, reduced hatch spacing, and selective multi-pass remelting). Ensure identical powder characteristics and environmental conditions. Produce multiple replicates for statistical analysis.
measurements: Mechanical properties via tensile testing and microhardness measurements
Microstructural analysis using SEM and EBSD to quantify porosity and dislocation/grain distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens produced with the optimized parameters do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision and mechanical integrity, or if microstructural analyses do not demonstrate the predicted reduction in defect density compared to the baseline specimens, the hypothesis will be falsified.

During LPBF, a thin layer of metal powders is spread over a build platform and then selectively melted by a high-power laser source (Fig. 1a). Melting occurs sequentially as the laser is scanned back and forth in tracks that fill the areas to be consolidated. The H and L strategies differ in how close melt tracks are to one another within a single layer (i.e., the melt track area density), which is determined by the hatch spacing parameter, h. They also differ in how many times the same layer is scanned by the laser; namely whether the previously consolidated material is remelted or not. This foundational exploration aims to advance the application of this technology in fields such as surface engineering, additive manufacturing, and remanufacturing repairs. Future research will delve into the multi-pass and multi-layer laser cladding techniques for AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys and their microstructures and properties. Researchers and engineering practitioners can utilize the findings from this research to judiciously manage processing parameters based on the results of gray correlation analysis. The outcomes of multi-objective optimization can assist in the selection of appropriate process parameters aligned with specific application requirements. At the same time, numerical simulation techniques are applied to verify the rationality of optimization results, accurately predict the melting and solidification behavior of powders, reduce experimental costs and time, and thus accelerate the development process. In addition, the paper provides important references for the laser cladding process of other high-entropy alloy materials and offers ideas into the process analysis and optimization of other advanced manufacturing technologies.
